Metrics confirmed from the Lighthouse JSON (contact-us mobile, fetched 2026-10-31T01:02Z, simulated slow 4G, 4x CPU): performance 0.67, FCP 2.3 s, LCP 5.9 s, Speed Index 3.7 s, TBT 330 ms, total 764 KiB, unused JavaScript 132 KiB; desktop 0.85 with LCP 1.3 s. lcp-breakdown-insight names img.hero-bg (412x873, loading=lazy) as the LCP element (observed TTFB 417 ms, load delay 408 ms, load 105 ms, render delay 130 ms) and lcp-discovery-insight fails both 'fetchpriority=high should be applied' and 'LCP resources shouldn't use loading=lazy'; the HTML has 0 rel=preload (the server does send a 103 Early Hint preloading the CSS). Live DOM: Vector-2.svg is 202 KiB, loading="lazy", no fetchpriority, bounding box top 0 height 873 at 390, so the lazy attribute on an in-viewport image is real. Two cause details are wrong or overstated. First, the four GSAP tags (gsap.min.js, SplitText, TextPlugin, ScrollTrigger) and jQuery plus the webflow chunks are synchronous scripts at the END of the body (character offsets 24,096 to 25,416 of 28,401; only gtag and Finsweet attributes sit in the head, both async), not site-wide head code, so they do not delay the first render of the hero; Lighthouse still lists them under render-blocking-insight (estimated savings 1,060 ms) because they are parser-blocking in the body, but their real cost is TBT and main-thread time (bootup 1.0 s, gtag 353 ms and webflow chunk 366 ms are the biggest), not LCP. Second, in my own Playwright Chromium run on the live page (390x844, 1.6 Mbps, 150 ms RTT, 4x CPU via CDP) the PerformanceObserver reported the H1 as the LCP element at 1,292 ms and never promoted the full-viewport SVG, so in current Chrome the SVG may not be the field LCP element and un-lazying it may move Speed Index more than LCP. The page is still slow on mobile for a paid landing page (score 67), so high stands; the fix list should say footer code rather than head code, and should lead with the lazy hero image, the 195 KiB gtag payload and the 132 KiB of unused JavaScript.

Reproduced the mechanics at 1440x900 and 1024x768: the Webflow interaction sets inline color rgba(225,201,121,0.3) on h3.process-title and rgba(255,255,255,0.3) on p.process-text for steps away from the viewport centre (0.392 on the next one), and axe color-contrast reports 1.84 (#586f57 on #1d4849, 40 px) for the title and 2.33 (#617f80 on #1d4849, 18 px) for the text on the dimmed cards, exactly the values claimed. With reducedMotion: 'reduce' emulated the sampled inline colours were identical (0.392 and 0.3), matchMedia confirmed the preference, Webflow IX2 reducedMotion was false, and neither the page nor site.css contains a prefers-reduced-motion rule. At 390 no inline styles are applied and nothing fails. Where I disagree is severity and one detail: the dimmed state is transient and tied to scroll position (at 1440x900 the 3 steps nearest the centre are at full contrast and each step reaches full contrast as the reader scrolls to it), so a sequential reader never meets failing text; the failure affects people who read ahead, zoom out or use tall viewports. The reduced-motion point is weak because the effect is a colour fade, not movement, so prefers-reduced-motion is not the natural control for it. Raising the inactive floor to about 60% as recommended is still right; medium.
